old.text: Oregon's dig rules are ORS 757.542 to 757.562 and OAR chapter 952, written by the Oregon Utility Notification Center (Oregon 811). Pre-mark the dig area in white, then call at least 2 full business days and not more than 10 business days before digging. Do not start until you have "received a response from each operator of underground facilities in the area." Ticket life: the Center's 2026 Addendum says the rule was changed "from 45 days to 30 days," effective January 8, 2026. Older copies of the rule and the Center's own FAQ page still say 45 calendar days, so the current number is not confirmed. Until you check with Oregon 811, plan on 30 days. Past ticket life, call in a new locate request. Tolerance zone: 24 inches around the outside of the line on all sides. Use hand tools or other non-invasive methods there. Hit a line: tell the operator right away; gas or hazardous liquid release, call 911. Don't bury it without the operator's OK.

new.text: Minimum wage in Oregon (as of Nov 5, 2026): From July 1, 2026: $15.55 standard, $16.80 Portland metro, $14.55 non-urban counties; adjusted each July 1. The federal minimum is $7.25; the highest of federal, state and local rates that applies where the work is done must be paid. Overtime in Oregon on private jobs: 1.5x over 40 hours a week; long workdays alone do not trigger overtime for construction. Public works (prevailing wage) jobs are different. BOLI says overtime is due after 8 hours a day Monday to Friday, even under 40 hours in the week; on an established schedule of four 10-hour days (Monday to Thursday or Tuesday to Friday), after 10 hours a day; and for all hours worked on Saturdays, Sundays and six legal holidays (New Year's Day, Memorial Day, Independence Day, Labor Day, Thanksgiving, Christmas). Give workers the schedule in writing before work starts, or it is taken as five days. Paid travel and shop time tied to the public job counts toward the daily hours. Overtime rate: base rate x 1.5, plus the fringe. A union agreement with different overtime terms governs. Prevailing wage and union jobs usually pay well above the minimum. For a specific case, ask HR, a labor attorney or the Oregon Bureau of Labor and Industries (BOLI).

new.text: Minimum wage in Washington (as of Nov 5, 2026): $17.13 per hour in 2026; $17.73 on January 1, 2027 (announced September 30, 2026). Higher local rates include Seattle ($21.30 in 2026), SeaTac, Tukwila, Renton, Bellingham, Everett, Burien and unincorporated King County. Exempt salary 2026: $80,168.40 a year; 2027: $92,196 (51+ employees) or $82,976.40 (50 or fewer). The federal minimum is $7.25; the highest of federal, state and local rates that applies where the work is done must be paid. Overtime in Washington on private jobs: 1.5x over 40 hours a week; long workdays alone do not trigger overtime. Public works jobs are different: on work for the state, a county or a city, done by contract or subcontract, 8 hours is a day's work and time over 8 hours in a day is paid at 1.5x (RCW 49.28.010). A 4-10 schedule avoids overtime for the first 2 hours over 8 only under a voluntary agreement written, signed and dated with each worker for that project (or a union agreement), kept 3 years; on it, no more than 10 hours a day except in an extraordinary emergency (WAC 296-127-022, RCW 49.28.065). Saturday, Sunday and holiday work still follows the prevailing wage overtime rules, and hours over 40 in a week are always overtime. Prevailing wage and union jobs usually pay well above the minimum. For a specific case, ask HR, a labor attorney or the Washington State Department of Labor and Industries (L&I).

old.text: Survey stake and flagging colors vary by company and job, so no single color chart is universal; ask the surveyor's legend. Common practice: pink, orange or fluorescent flagging on survey stakes; blue tops for finished grade hubs; red or other colors for other grades. Utility locate marks follow the APWA uniform color code: white proposed excavation, pink temporary survey marks, red electric, yellow gas, oil or steam, orange communications and CATV, blue potable water, purple reclaimed water and irrigation, green sewer and storm drain. Survey paint is not a utility locate.

Common practice: pink, orange or fluorescent flagging on survey stakes, and colored tops on grade hubs, but what each top color means changes by agency and region. On many jobs a blue top is a finished grade hub; WSDOT, for one, calls subgrade hubs blue tops, base rock hubs red tops and top course hubs yellow tops. Confirm which grade a top color means before you trim to it. Utility locate marks follow the APWA uniform color code: white proposed excavation, pink temporary survey marks, red electric, yellow gas, oil or steam, orange communications and CATV, blue potable water, purple reclaimed water and irrigation, green sewer and storm drain. old.text: The offset distance is usually written at the top of the lath, above the description: "10 / SD", "5 / WALL / WF". Many surveyors draw a circle around the offset number (a circled 5 = 5 ft off whatever the stake names); others write O/S or OS, or underline the offset twice, or put it above a line. L/O means line only: the stake is good for line, not for distance. A number in front of a slash on a utility lath is an offset distance, never a pipe size.

old.text: The common rule (from the Ten States Standards and state rules such as Virginia's) is that water mains should be at least 10 ft horizontally from sanitary sewers and sewer manholes, measured edge to edge. Under Virginia's rule, where local conditions prevent 10 ft, the water main may be closer if its bottom is at least 18 inches above the top of the sewer; if that can't be done, the sewer must be built of water-main-grade pipe and pressure tested in place, or the department may approve concrete encasement or another barrier. Water pipes must not pass through or touch any part of a sewer manhole. States vary on the details and on rules for storm sewers and force mains, so check your state rules and project specs.
old.title: Water and sewer separation: horizontal 10 ft rule

old.text: At crossings, the common rule is at least 18 inches of vertical separation between the bottom of the water main and the top of the sewer, with the water main above the sewer. Per Virginia's rule (Ten States approach): where that can't be met, sewers crossing over or under water mains must be built of water-main-grade pipe for 10 ft each side of the crossing. If the water main must go under the sewer, you need at least 18 inches between the bottom of the sewer and top of the water main, structural support for the sewer so it can't settle onto the main, and a full length of water pipe centered on the crossing so its joints are as far from the sewer as possible. Practical tip: when laying water main across a sewer, center a full stick on the crossing. Check your state and utility rules, which can differ.

old.text: California (Cal/OSHA) requires a protective system for each employee in an excavation unless it is made entirely in stable rock, or it is less than 5 feet deep and a competent person's examination of the ground finds no sign of a potential cave-in (8 CCR 1541.1(a)(1)). That is the same 5 ft test as federal OSHA. California's sloping table (8 CCR 1541.1 Appendix B) has the same slopes as the federal one. What California adds is a permit: 8 CCR 1539 sends excavation and trench permits to 8 CCR 341, and the app's state table (checked 2026-11-19) carries it as a Cal/OSHA permit for trenches or excavations 5 ft or deeper that a person enters, with emergency repair of underground facilities exempt. Section 341 itself was not re-read on 2026-11-20, so the permit details are not confirmed here beyond that. The trench shield rule matches the federal one: dig no more than 2 feet below the bottom of the support (8 CCR 1541.1(e)(2)(A)).
old.title: California trench protection depth and the Cal/OSHA excavation permit
old.topic: State safety plan: trench and excavation
old.edition: Title 8 CCR, section text read 2026-11-20 (Register 2011, No. 50)

new.text: California (Cal/OSHA) requires a protective system for each employee in an excavation unless it is made entirely in stable rock, or it is less than 5 feet deep and a competent person's examination of the ground finds no sign of a potential cave-in (8 CCR 1541.1(a)(1)). That is the same 5 ft test as federal OSHA. California's sloping table (8 CCR 1541.1 Appendix B) has the same slopes as the federal one. What California adds is a permit: 8 CCR 1539 sends excavation and trench permits to 8 CCR 341, which requires a Cal/OSHA permit before building a trench or excavation 5 ft or deeper into which any person is required to descend (341(d)(5)(A)); trenches for emergency repair of underground facilities are exempt (341(e)). The trench shield rule matches the federal one: dig no more than 2 feet below the bottom of the support (8 CCR 1541.1(e)(2)(A)).

old.text: Paid rest breaks for adults (as of Nov 5, 2026): California, Colorado, Kentucky, Nevada, Oregon and Washington require 10 minutes per 4 hours worked (California, Colorado, Nevada and Oregon "or major fraction"); Minnesota 15 minutes per 4 consecutive hours (2026); Vermont "reasonable opportunities"; Illinois only for hotel room attendants. Every other state: no state law; federal rules apply (no rest break required, but short breaks given are paid). Daily overtime: California (over 8 h at 1.5x, over 12 h at 2x), Alaska (over 8 h, employers with 4+ employees), Nevada (over 8 h in 24 h for workers paid under 1.5x minimum wage, $18.00), Colorado (over 12 h). 7th-day premium: California and Kentucky. Every other state follows weekly overtime only (1.5x over 40). Local rules can be stricter: check the city or county. For a specific case, ask HR, a labor attorney or the state labor office.

old.text: South Carolina ticket types (SC811 Excavator Manual 2026): Normal; Design (operators have 15 full working days; no digging on it); Emergency; Large Project; Subaqueous (underwater: 10 working days' notice, tolerance zone 15 feet either side). Large Project: a job expected to take more than 90 days, or that meets the highway, development or utility size tests. Notify the center at least 30 days before starting; a planning meeting is held within 15 days; each phase gets its own start and end dates and needs no updates while work stays inside them. Emergency: "any sudden or unforeseen event that requires immediate action." Notify SC811 and the operators as soon as practicable; operators make contact within three hours. Calling it an emergency does not remove liability for damage. Bad weather: ice or snow can be an extraordinary circumstance that lets an operator post Code 110 with a later marking date. Complaints: file with the Attorney General's Office within 45 days of the incident. Fine amounts are not in the manual and were not confirmed.
